archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, leaky secondary)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff under Jeff Hafley running a ground-heavy offense around Malik Willis while a defense that ranked 8th in EPA two years ago has fallen to the bottom of the league, and the 1-6 record is an honest reflection of a roster in teardown.

report.headline: An honest 1-6: a broken pass defense and leaky protection, not bad luck
report.take:
Miami is not an unlucky team. The point differential implies about 1.5 wins, against one actual win, and the net EPA (30th) agrees with the standings. This is Hafley's first year, Willis has started every game, and the identity is clear: run the ball, stay out of long passing downs, and hope the defense gets off the field. The pass rate over expected is -9.6, 31st in the league, so this is about as run-committed as any offense in football.

The record comes down to the defense. Opponents post 0.299 EPA per dropback, dead last, and the success rate allowed is also last. On third down opponents convert 52.1%, 31st. The pass rush barely exists, with a pressure rate 22nd and a sack rate 27th, so quarterbacks get time and easy completions. The offense can't make up the difference. Its line opens early lanes, with 3.2 yards before contact (3rd), but it gets stuffed often (28th) and allows pressure at the league's 30th-worst rate, while Willis holds the ball longer than any quarterback in the league. Special teams cost almost three points a game on top of that.

The raw numbers hide the shape of the problem. The 340.7 yards allowed per game is a middling 16th, which makes the defense look average until you see that opponents don't need yards. They stay on schedule and convert. The secondary has actually erased opposing WR1s, who score 7.5 PPR points under their norm (2nd). The damage comes from tight ends and backs underneath and from third receivers, where the EPA allowed ranks last at both TE1 and WR3. Opponents have worked out that the middle of the field is open. History says this has been building: the 2023 team ranked 5th in net EPA, 2025 slid to 27th, and now 30th.

The path is slightly better than the start. After three lopsided September losses, Miami has stayed within one score every week, won at New York, and the passing game has had positive EPA in two of its last three games. That is real but modest progress. The roster is still built for a top-five pick, not a turnaround.

strengths.title: Run blocking that wins early
strengths.body: Miami's backs get 3.2 yards before contact, 3rd in the league, and the staff leans on it harder than almost anyone. When it works it can carry a game, as in the 217-yard rushing day against Cincinnati. The weakness is the all-or-nothing results: the high stuff rate means drives stall when the early lanes close, so this will stay a volatile strength.

strengths.title: Top receivers get taken away
strengths.body: Opposing WR1s score 7.5 PPR points below their usual output, 2nd-best in the league. The boundary coverage on the No. 1 option holds up. The catch is that it pushes targets to tight ends and backs, who get more of the targets against Miami than the league norm. The strength is real, but it doesn't make the pass defense good.

strengths.title: Competitive since September
strengths.body: After double-digit losses in each of the first three weeks, Miami has covered in Weeks 4, 7 and 8 and pushed in Week 5. Willis posted +11.4 passing EPA in the win over the Jets. This is a team losing closer games rather than a good one, but the floor has risen.

concerns.title: The league's worst pass defense
concerns.body: Miami is last in EPA allowed per dropback and last in success rate, and it lets opponents convert third downs 52.1% of the time. A weak rush and soft coverage underneath produce it together: tight ends gain 0.89 EPA a target, last in the league. The defense ranked 25th in EPA last year too, so this is a multi-year roster problem, not a slump.

concerns.title: Pressure and a long clock
concerns.body: The line allows pressure at the 30th-worst rate and a sack rate that ranks 27th. Willis compounds it by holding the ball longest in the league. Some of that is a scrambler's style, but it caps the dropback game and turns third-and-long into a sack threat. It gets worse this week with a full-time tackle out.

concerns.title: Special teams bleeding points
concerns.body: The kicking and return units lose almost three points a game, 30th in the league. For a team that has lost three games by a single score, that is often the margin. Nothing suggests a quick fix.

trend.note: Three blowout losses opened the season. Since then every game has been within one score, including the Jets win, and the passing EPA has turned positive in two of the last three. The rise is real but is starting from a very low floor.

nextGame.headline: A shootout total against a team that can't win shootouts
nextGame.body:
Detroit is lopsided: its offense is 3rd in EPA and its passing game 3rd, scoring 30.7 a game, while its defense is 31st in EPA and allows the most yards in the league. That sets up a 50.5 total, well above where Miami's games usually land. Miami's best hope is to drag Detroit into a slower, run-heavy game. Detroit has been a poor bet to cover, with an ATS rate of 0.2 that ranks 30th, and Miami gets 7 at home.

Availability cuts both ways. Miami loses tackle Kadyn Proctor, an every-snap starter, to a concussion, against a Lions rush that already has 21 sacks, 2nd in the league. Reserve end Malik Herring is questionable. Detroit's defense is far more banged up. Linebacker Jack Campbell, a 97%-snap player, is doubtful after a hospital stay with a neck injury. Corner D.J. Reed is questionable with a hip, safety Brian Branch and linebacker DJ Wonnum are questionable after concussions, and safety Kerby Joseph has been ruled out. The middle of Detroit's defense could be thin.

waysToWin.title: Attack Detroit's thinned middle
waysToWin.body: Detroit already allows the 31st-worst EPA to tight ends, and Campbell, Branch and Joseph may all be missing from the second level. That is the area Greg Dulcich and Malik Washington work. Quick throws over the middle also take the ball out of Willis's hands before Detroit's rush gets home.

waysToWin.title: Shorten the game on the ground
waysToWin.body: Miami's run-first approach and early lanes, 3rd in yards before contact, can keep Jared Goff on the sideline. Detroit is only middling against the run, 16th in rush EPA allowed. Fewer possessions is the classic underdog script against an elite offense.

waysToWin.title: Keep it within a score late
waysToWin.body: Detroit rarely covers, and Miami has hung within one score every week since September. A tight game makes a backdoor result or a late upset possible.

waysToLose.title: Goff picks apart the secondary
waysToLose.body: The league's 3rd-best passing offense meets the league's worst pass defense. Detroit also funnels targets to tight ends, exactly where Miami bleeds. If Miami can't get off the field on third down, the game gets away early.

waysToLose.title: Protection collapses without Proctor
waysToLose.body: Miami's line already ranks 30th in pressure allowed, and its quarterback holds the ball longest in the league. Now it loses a 100%-snap tackle against a top-seven pressure defense. Sacks and drive-killing negative plays are the most likely way the offense stalls.

waysToLose.title: Losing the hidden yardage
waysToLose.body: Detroit's special teams are 2nd in EPA, while Miami's are 30th. The field-position swing could decide a game that Detroit is already favored to win.

nextGame.watch: How Miami protects Willis without Proctor. If the replacement holds up and the ball comes out quickly to Dulcich, Miami can stay in it; if the Lions' rush lives in the backfield, it won't be close.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying numbers match the record, so don't expect a big bounce. What is sustainable is a team that loses closer games than it did in September, built on the run game and on coverage of No. 1 receivers. The pass defense and the pass protection are structural problems that won't fix themselves in-season. The schedule has three clear chances in Indianapolis, the Jets at home and the winless Chargers at home. Two games against Buffalo's top-ranked offense and trips to Denver and Green Bay look like losses.

The turnover margin is mildly negative and special teams are bad. Neither is driving a hidden collapse that will regress the other way. Expect a finish in the low-to-mid single digits in wins and a high draft pick. The real question for Hafley's first year is whether the defense gets from bottom-three to merely bad.
swingFactors: Whether the pass defense can stop leaking to tight ends and backs
Pass protection and Willis's time to throw
Winning the soft games vs IND, NYJ and LAC

confidence.note: Seven games is a small sample, but the record, point differential and EPA all agree, and the decline matches last season.
